Skip next section Two suspected IS members detained in NRW 08/06/2026 August 6, 2026 Two suspected IS members detained in NRW Two Iraqi nationals have been arrested on suspicion of terrorism by German authorities. The arrests took place after evidence emerged that they had fought with the so-called Islamic State in Iraq a decade ago. The arrests were made in the towns of Höxter and Bottrop in the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia. Cell phones and laptops were seized from the detainees' apartments. The men, aged 29 and 46, have been accused of being members of a terrorist organization abroad, a spokeswoman for the Düsseldorf State Prosecutor's Office said. She added that the Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA) received a tip and was then able to track down the suspects. Authorities have not yet decided whether the men would be held in pretrial detention. There are no indications that either of them was involved in any planned attacks in Germany, the spokeswoman added. "This is a serious attack on transport and logistical infrastructure in Germany," the Office of the Federal Prosecutor said as it announced it was taking the lead. The €3 billion ($3.46 billion) subsidy scheme was introduced by Germany's conservative-led coalition government to incentivize consumers to purchase and lease electric cars, certain plug-in hybrids and EVs fitted with range extenders. According to the Federal Motor Transport Authority (KBA), the Chinese manufacturer BYD was one of those who benefited. BYD registered sales of 5,240 new cars in Germany in July, more than four and a half times as many cars in July of the previous year. "While the strong growth in electric cars is accelerating the ramp-up of electromobility in Germany, it has so far brought only limited benefits to the domestic automotive industry ," said auto expert Constantin Gall of the consulting firm EY, adding that Chinese companies are the main beneficiaries. The high demand for electric cars has been a boost for the entire new-car market in Germany. German pilot Klaus Plasa was at the controls for its flight earlier in the week. The FW 190 went into service in 1941 and was a heavier plane than its better-known counterpart, the Messerschmitt Bf 109, and less comfortable at high altitudes. But this also made it a much more versatile aircraft, capable of flying longer distances and carrying more firepower and fuel. The aircraft was downed in France in 1944. Its wreckage was taken to the US in 2000. Restoration work began there, but the aircraft never regained operational status. Turkish aerobatic pilot Ali İsmet Öztürk led the team that disassembled and restored the aircraft so it was airworthy once more Image: Luft- und Raumfahrtmuseum Eskisehir/dpa/picture alliance The Turkish aviation club acquired the plane in 2023 and an 11-member team set to work restoring it over roughly 14 months. In the early 20th century, Germany had helped modernize the military, including the air force, of what was then the Ottoman Empire. This collaboration continued in the early years of the Republic of Turkey. By 1948, three years after Nazi Germany's defeat and with spare parts in short supply, Turkey — which by then was starting to eye an alliance with the US and membership in what would become NATO — retired its remaining FW 190 fleet. The Sivrihisar Aviation Club Association said it wanted to preserve the countries' shared aviation heritage. It plans to display the rare aircraft at an air show in Eskisehir in September.
